To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

nerve growth factor receptors (NGFR) are present in the adult rat spinal cord, in both large motoneurons and in a population of small neurons, and that NGFR expression is rapidly induced in motoneurons by peripheral nerve lesion.
the expression of the NGF receptor in adult motoneurons is modulated after peripheral nerve lesions, and that the time course of the response is different for crush and cut lesions.
the number of motoneurons expressing LNGFR in the normal adult rat increases with age and that, following peripheral axotomy, motoneurons rapidly and transiently re‐express LNGFR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of nerve growth factor (NGF) in the regulation of neuronal growth and development.
the study of the neurobiological basis of the development and regeneration of the neuromuscular system.
the role played by the NGF family of growth factors (NGF, BDNF and NT‐3) in the survival and maintenance of the adult motoneuron.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

LNGFR is expressed in the normal adult spinal neurons, but that its re‐expression after peripheral axonal injury is a transient phenomenon that is dependent upon the presence of a functional target for axonal regeneration.
LNGFR expression is not only an important developmental phenomenon, but is also a marker for axotomized adult spinal motoneurons.

(1) the LNGFR‐IR phenotype of motoneurons in the adult rat spinal cord is not limited to a small number of large motoneuronal populations, but is also expressed by a large number of small neurons; (2) the LNGFR response of motoneurons after peripheral nerve lesion is a rapid, transient, and massive event; (3) in the case of a crush lesion, the LNGFR response is not limited to the motoneurons of a single peripheral nerve
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, after peripheral nerve lesions, motoneurons re‐express the LNGFR and that this re‐expression may be related to the ability of the motoneurons to survive and regenerate after axotomy.

, in the rat, the re‐expression and disappearance of LNGFR is a rapid process, which is not related to the presence of a neuroma or the reconnection of the motoneurons to the muscle, but rather to the presence of the target muscle and its innervation by the motoneuron.

the re‐expression in adult rat spinal motoneurons of LNGFR‐like immunoreactivity after axotomy by peripheral lesions is a rapid, massive and short‐lived phenomenon, which is not dependent on axonal re‐innervation and is not related to motoneuron death.
The main takeaway from our work is that

nerve growth factor receptor immunostaining in the adult rat spinal cord is not a static phenomenon, but rather is subject to rapid changes in response to peripheral nerve lesions, and that these changes are not simply a reflection of the regenerating state of the lesioned motoneurons, but are also dependent on the type of lesion and its outcome.

the expression of LNGFR on axotomized neurons is not a permanent feature of motoneurons, but is a dynamic response to the axotomized state of these cells, and is modulated by the presence of an intact nerve.
nerve growth factor receptors can be expressed in adult motoneurons in response to injury.
